extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants / biomedical researchers writing NIH research proposals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing the 'Potential Pitfalls' / 'Alternative Approaches' part of an NIH Research Plan: what to include, how to frame it, and how much space to devote. Targets presentation, tone, and content to satisfy study-section reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a Potential Pitfalls / Alternative Considerations section
rubrics_metrics.description: Many study sections (including all the ones the author has sat on) expect to see a 'Potential Pitfalls' or 'Alternative Considerations' section in the Research Plan and will ding you if you don't include it; it is a common 'StockCritique.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do include such a section so reviewers can find evidence you considered adverse outcomes; omission may lead to negative comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not dismiss pitfalls as impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid coming across as 'This is some possible outcome that would really screw with my hypotheses and interpretations. However it ain't gonna happen, because of blahdeblah blah, so let's not worry about that.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defensive/dismissive stance is an anti-pattern; if that is your only answer, choose a different pitfall to discuss or revise the plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fully acknowledge plausible pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that a pitfall you identify (or that is overwhelmingly obvious) could possibly occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly acknowledge plausibility rather than dismissing it; this builds credibility with reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe how a pitfall would change interpretation and future work
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a description of how an identified pitfall occurring would change your interpretation of the experiment's results and how it would change the subsequent line of attack; perhaps show how working hypotheses might need to be modified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific about consequences and next steps so reviewers see you have thought through implications and contingency plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide reasonable contingency / alternative approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that you have a reasonable plan to advance should adverse outcomes occur (i.e., alternative approaches or follow-up experiments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame alternatives as concrete, feasible next steps that preserve the project's goals; the reviewer should be able to say 'The applicant appropriately considered potential adverse outcomes and pitfalls and has a reasonable plan to advance should they occur.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose which pitfalls to discuss; don't ignore the obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: You get to choose which pitfalls you talk about. You can't leave something that is overwhelmingly obvious to any reader ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select pitfalls strategically: cover the obvious high-impact ones, but avoid listing a long laundry list. If you have too many obvious pitfalls, the plan may need serious redesign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer problem-centric alternatives over technique-centric ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Make both your 'main approach' and 'alternative approach' problem-centric, not technique-centric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows you're focused on the hypothesis/problem rather than merely applying techniques A or B, and leaves the impression the approach is comprehensive and well thought-out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider labeling the section 'Alternative Approaches' to reduce negative framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the 'alternatives' designation removes negative spin from an 'adverse outcome' discussion and makes it easier to show you've considered disconfirming possibilities without sounding alarmist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: describe a surprising/paradoxical outcome and present it as worthy of further investigation rather than as a fatal flaw. This framing can be terse and constructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the section concise due to limited page real estate
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep this section to a bare minimum (one paragraph or less) when space is tight in the proposal format; if you run out of space, this is often among the first things to cut.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize preliminary data and core experimental design; use minimal text to convey plausible pitfalls and succinct contingency plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of anticipated results is distinct and necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of interpretation of anticipated results is necessary and distinct from the pitfalls/alternatives section and is part of convincing the study section that your experiments are well-designed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure you include clear interpretation plans for outcomes as part of the Research Plan, not just brief pitfall avoidance language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative importance depends on overall strength of proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: If the experiments are viewed as highly significant, innovative, and well-designed, reviewers may be less likely to ding you over this section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't rely on this — write the section well when possible — but recognize its weight is modulated by the perceived overall quality and excitement of the proposed work.
